purpose: One row per broken decision, with the suite that noticed and the case that failed. Every suite named here was run UNMUTATED and green before the first mutation was applied -- a kill is only evidence if the suite passes on a clean tree. Re-runnable: node scripts/run-win272-mutations.mjs. A SURVIVOR is recorded as one and never explained away, and a mutation the compiler refuses is counted apart from a kill because a type error is evidence the type layer holds rather than evidence a case noticed. A row whose suite TIMED OUT is counted apart from both, because a mutation that hangs a suite is not one that kills it.

rows.subject: the client's own duplicate suppression
rows.breaks: a redelivery of the frame at exactly the last applied position is APPLIED again, which is the double-apply the acceptance forbids
cases: admitting a frame against the last one applied > calls a redelivery a duplicate rather than a gap
admitting a frame against the last one applied > conserves a whole run: every frame is applied exactly once

rows.subject: gap detection
rows.breaks: a frame that skips ahead is applied, so a client renders a partial answer it believes is whole
cases: admitting a frame against the last one applied > reports a gap with the number of frames missing

rows.subject: the reserved-field refusal
rows.breaks: a payload field named `seq` overwrites the sequence ON THE WIRE, so the producer chooses the client's gap detection
cases: the flat frame > refuses every reserved field a payload could shadow, one at a time
the flat frame > does not let a payload field named `seq` rewrite the sequence

rows.subject: why a stream stopped
rows.breaks: a `stream.offline` frame with no cursor of its own classifies as `severed` rather than `interrupted`, so the reader loses the fact that the SERVER let it go on purpose -- the one distinction an operator needs to tell a policy decision from a crash
cases: why a stream stopped > falls back to the reader's position when the offline frame carries none
why a stream stopped > gives every terminal frame type a classification that is not `severed`

rows.subject: the cursor's control-character refusal
rows.breaks: a stream id carrying a newline is encoded into an SSE `id:` line, which injects a field into every reader's byte stream
cases: the resume cursor > refuses a stream id carrying a control character

rows.subject: the length-prefixed cursor
rows.breaks: the delimiter reappears between the id and the sequence, so an id holding the delimiter decodes to the wrong position
cases: the resume cursor > round-trips a plain id
the resume cursor > round-trips an id holding the delimiter and digits
the resume cursor > round-trips through the two encodings a real `Last-Event-ID` survives

rows.subject: M0.4 decision D4 AS CORRECTED
rows.breaks: an absent `sv` defaults to 1 on a NEW surface too, which is the uncorrected proposal and makes the version field optional everywhere
cases: negotiating the schema version > defaults an absent version to 1 at a legacy ingress and refuses it elsewhere

rows.subject: the per-frame byte ceiling
rows.breaks: a frame of any size is admitted, so one tool result becomes a memory incident in every connected browser
cases: frame size > admits a frame at the ceiling and refuses one past it
frame size > counts BYTES, so a multi-byte alphabet cannot buy extra room
frame size > honours a caller's tighter limit

rows.subject: whether a client reconnects
rows.breaks: a client polls a finished stream forever, because a completed turn is reported as resumable
cases: why a stream stopped > resumes on exactly the two ends that can still grow

rows.subject: THE CONSERVATION REFUSAL
rows.breaks: a cursor whose frames were trimmed is answered with a PAGE, so the client receives a gap dressed as a sequence and renders state that is silently missing the middle
cases: backpressure: a consumer slower than the producer > REFUSES a trimmed cursor rather than answering with a gap that looks complete
backpressure: a consumer slower than the producer > serves the boundary cursor — the oldest frame still held minus one

rows.subject: the trim boundary, off by one
rows.breaks: a reader that is exactly caught up is REFUSED, so every reader at the boundary is disconnected instead of served
cases: backpressure: a consumer slower than the producer > serves the boundary cursor — the oldest frame still held minus one

rows.subject: no frames after a terminal frame
rows.breaks: a producer can append after the seal, which is the trailing-invalid-frames case the acceptance forbids
cases: sealing > refuses an append after the seal

rows.subject: the first seal wins
rows.breaks: HSET OVERWRITES where HSETNX claims: a second seal replaces the first and still reports `already-sealed`, so a retry turns a completed turn into a failed one AND tells the caller it did not
cases: sealing > tells a reader the producer finished, and the first seal wins
two clients, one server > lets only one of two racing seals win, and both learn the same outcome

rows.subject: the length bound
rows.breaks: one runaway stream is unbounded, so a single turn can evict every other stream's frames from the server
cases: backpressure: a consumer slower than the producer > REFUSES a trimmed cursor rather than answering with a gap that looks complete
backpressure: a consumer slower than the producer > serves the boundary cursor — the oldest frame still held minus one
backpressure: a consumer slower than the producer > reads from the beginning without claiming continuity, and the client sees the gap

rows.subject: reads are STRICTLY after the cursor
rows.breaks: a resuming reader is handed the frame it already holds, which is a duplicate on every reconnect
cases: append and read back > reads STRICTLY after a cursor, so a resuming client never sees its own last frame
append and read back > honours the page limit and lets a caller walk the whole stream
sealing > surfaces the seal on every page, including one a reader has already caught up past
backpressure: a consumer slower than the producer > still serves a cursor inside the retained window
following the live end > returns as soon as a frame arrives rather than after the whole window
following the live end > returns an empty page when the window closes with nothing written

rows.subject: at-least-once delivery
rows.breaks: a handler that rejects never sees the event again, so a partial failure silently loses it
cases: at-least-once > redelivers the same event after a handler rejects, and does not skip ahead
at-least-once > moves past a poison event rather than stopping the subscription forever

rows.subject: a fan-out seam is not a queue
rows.breaks: a subscriber catches up on events published before it existed, which makes the bus a second canonical store beside the outbox
cases: this is a fan-out seam and not a queue > does NOT deliver an event published before the subscriber existed

rows.subject: the handshake wait is BOUNDED
rows.breaks: the wait for a server that is not there yet is a day rather than a bounded window, so the FIRST command against a cold connection HANGS instead of failing closed -- and the caller that was written to report `unavailable` reports nothing at all
cases: a server that is not there yet > recovers once the server appears, rather than failing forever on one early error

rows.subject: backpressure
rows.breaks: a full socket is written to without bound, so a slow browser becomes unbounded heap in this process
cases: backpressure > GIVES UP on a socket that never drains, rather than waiting forever
the pump > reports a slow consumer without writing anything else to it

rows.subject: THE CREDENTIAL EXPIRY FENCE
rows.breaks: the fence is a day past the credential's expiry, so a stream outlives the credential that opened it -- which is the unbounded case the live lane has
cases: the pump > STOPS AT THE CREDENTIAL EXPIRY, and reports the position it reached

rows.subject: at most ONE terminal frame
rows.breaks: a completed stream gets a SECOND terminal frame after the producer's own, which is the duplicate the acceptance forbids and the exact defect in `streaming.service.ts`
cases: the terminal frame a client receives > is written for exactly four endings and for no others

rows.subject: the tenancy boundary IS the journal key
rows.breaks: a stream id becomes a bearer capability across environments, so naming one environment reaches another's frames
cases: the journal key is the tenancy boundary > puts the environment inside the key rather than beside it

rows.subject: the scope is the AUTHORIZATION's, never the path's
rows.breaks: a forged scope is honoured, because the key is built from the caller's own path segment rather than from the scope tenancy re-derived

rows.subject: encode, then write, then advance
rows.breaks: a frame that was not written advances the position, so a resuming client is handed the frame AFTER the one it never received
cases: the pump > reports a slow consumer without writing anything else to it

rows.subject: a terminal frame a client will APPLY
rows.breaks: the terminal frame is numbered 0, which every correct client's `admitFrame` calls a DUPLICATE and drops — leaving it with no explanation for a stream that stopped

rows.subject: authorization happens BEFORE the journal is touched
rows.breaks: the four-gate RBAC decision is skipped entirely, so an authenticated operator with NO membership in the organization reads another tenant's frames -- and the refusal that would have named which gate closed never happens

rows.subject: the guest session's server-side expiry fence
rows.breaks: a captured Cookie header is admitted for as long as the platform token behind it lives, so the lifetime is enforced only by the browser that chooses to send it -- which is the defect this tranche closed
cases: the guest session's LIFETIME is now enforced by the server and not only by the browser > REFUSES A REPLAYED COOKIE PAST ITS OWN EXPIRY, without contacting the agent

rows.subject: the same-origin gate on a SameSite=None credential
rows.breaks: any site can POST a guest turn with the visitor's own partitioned cookie: the Origin comparison IS the CSRF defence here, and dropping it leaves only a content type an attacker sets themselves
cases: the stream's refusals are the security boundary, and every one is reached first > refuses a CROSS-ORIGIN mutation with 403 and never contacts the agent
the stream's refusals are the security boundary, and every one is reached first > refuses a mutation with NO Origin header at all

rows.subject: the cookie scope hash binding a session to one agent AND one environment
rows.breaks: one agent's guest session is accepted against every environment it exists in, so a session minted in staging reads production
cases: the stream's refusals are the security boundary, and every one is reached first > REFUSES A COOKIE MINTED FOR ANOTHER ENVIRONMENT on the same agent

rows.subject: CHIPS partitioning on the embed credential
rows.breaks: the guest cookie joins the unpartitioned jar, so every embedding site shares one visitor's session instead of each getting its own
cases: the unauthenticated mint refuses before it spends an upstream round trip > writes a cookie a browser will keep out of script, off plaintext and out of a third party's jar

rows.subject: the legacy value shape, which is the only thing an old browser still holds
rows.breaks: a value with no expiry prefix is admitted unbounded, which re-opens exactly the hole the prefix closed -- and does it for every cookie already in a browser
cases: the guest session's LIFETIME is now enforced by the server and not only by the browser > refuses a value with no expiry prefix — the shape minted before this fence existed

rows.subject: the rate-limit key on an UNAUTHENTICATED mint
rows.breaks: every guest-token mint arrives at the agent from the BFF's own address, so the per-IP bucket -- the only defence an unauthenticated mint has -- counts the whole internet as one caller
cases: the unauthenticated mint refuses before it spends an upstream round trip > forwards the rate-limit key and NOT the visitor's own cookie jar

rows.subject: the visitor's disconnect reaching the agent
rows.breaks: a visitor closing the tab leaves the agent's turn running to completion against a socket nobody is reading, which is the leak a public guest surface can be pointed at
cases: a guest that closes the tab mid-stream > TEARS THE AGENT'S TURN DOWN rather than leaving it streaming into nothing

rows.subject: the refusal that must not reflect the agent's own bytes
rows.breaks: an upstream failure's detail -- provider error codes, and in the case this suite scripts a provider key -- is handed to an anonymous visitor
cases: a stream that ends because the turn finished is distinguishable from one that died > reports an upstream refusal WITHOUT reflecting the agent's own bytes

rows.subject: the anti-buffering directive that makes a proxied stream a stream
rows.breaks: an intermediary is free to gzip the event stream, which buffers it: the visitor gets the whole turn at the end, indistinguishable from a stream that never streamed
cases: a stream that ends because the turn finished is distinguishable from one that died > ends cleanly on the agent's own terminal frame, with the anti-buffering headers a proxy needs

rows.subject: the mint's refusal to hand a browser a half-minted session
rows.breaks: an agent answering without a token still produces a Set-Cookie, so the browser holds a guest session whose value is the literal text undefined and every later turn 401s with no way to recover
cases: the unauthenticated mint refuses before it spends an upstream round trip > writes NO cookie when the agent answers with a half-minted session
